questions.question_text: A radio station invites listeners to phone in and vote for the song of the year. Which type of bias arises because listeners decide for themselves whether to phone in?

options.text: Volunteer bias, because only listeners who feel strongly enough to call take part.
Selection bias, because the station chose which listeners to call.
options.why: The station chose nobody — the listeners chose themselves, which is what makes this volunteer bias.

options.text: Survivorship bias, because only songs still being played can be voted for.
options.why: Survivorship bias is about failures missing from the data collected, not about which songs are available to vote for.

options.text: Small sample size, because a phone-in poll collects only a few responses.
options.why: A phone-in can collect thousands of votes; the defect named here is who chose to take part, not how many did.

questions.solution_text:
Listeners choose for themselves whether to phone in, so the votes come from the listeners with the strongest opinions.
**Volunteer bias.**

questions.question_text: A phone-case company measures how long its cases last by inspecting the cases customers bring in for a free upgrade after two years. Cases that broke earlier were thrown away. Which type of bias arises from the fact that the broken cases can never appear in the data?

options.text: Survivorship bias, because only the cases that lasted two years are inspected.
Volunteer bias, because customers decide whether to come in for the upgrade.
options.why: Names how customers arrive rather than the missing broken cases, which is the mechanism the question pins down.

options.text: Selection bias, because the company inspects cases only at its own stores.
options.why: Where the inspection happens is not the problem; the broken cases are missing however many stores are used.

options.text: Small sample size, because only upgrade customers are inspected.
options.why: Confuses a restricted group with too few responses; the group could be huge and still contain no broken case.

questions.solution_text:
Cases that broke early were thrown away, so they can never be inspected and only the cases that lasted are in the data.
**Survivorship bias.**

questions.question_text: A club president asks $3$ of the club's $260$ members whether the meeting night should change, then reports that the members want the change. Which type of bias is this?

options.text: Small sample size, because three members cannot show the range of views held by $260$.
Volunteer bias, because the three members agreed to answer the question.
options.why: Answering a question you were asked is not volunteering to join a survey; the defect is that only three members were asked.

options.text: Survivorship bias, because former members of the club were not asked.
options.why: Former members are outside the group being investigated; the defect is the number of current members asked.

options.text: Selection bias, because the president asked members he already knows well.
options.why: Nothing in the report says how the three were chosen, only that there were three of them.

questions.solution_text:
Only $3$ of the $260$ members were asked, which is far too few to show the variety of opinion in the club.
**Small sample size.**

questions.question_text: A review form asks: 'Most customers say our new coffee machine is excellent. What do you think?' Which fault does this question have?

options.text: It is a leading question, because it tells the customer what most people think before asking.
It is an ambiguous question, because no time period is given.
options.why: A missing time period makes a question ambiguous, but nothing here asks how often; the fault is the opinion supplied first.

options.text: It offers not enough choices, because the customer answers in their own words.
options.why: An open question allows any answer rather than too few, so the fault is not in the options.

options.text: It creates volunteer bias, because customers choose whether to reply.
options.why: Names a fault in who replies rather than in the wording, which is what the question asks about.

questions.solution_text:
Stating that most customers already call the machine excellent pushes the customer towards agreeing.
**A leading question.**

questions.question_text: A questionnaire asks: 'How many times do you order takeaway?' with a box in which to write a number. Which fault does this question have?

options.text: It is ambiguous, because no time period is given.
It is a leading question, because it suggests that ordering takeaway is normal.
options.why: The wording supplies no opinion and no one-sided information; the fault is the missing time period.

options.text: It offers not enough choices, because only a number may be written.
options.why: A free number box allows any answer, so the choices are not restricted.

options.text: It creates survivorship bias, because people who never order takeaway are ignored.
options.why: Someone who never orders can write $0$, so nobody is excluded by the box.

questions.solution_text:
'How many times' has no time period attached, so one person answers per week and another per year.
**An ambiguous question.**

questions.question_text: A questionnaire asks how satisfied a customer was with a delivery, offering only **Satisfied**, **Very satisfied** and **Extremely satisfied**. Which fault does this question have?

options.text: It offers not enough choices, because there is no neutral or negative option.
It is ambiguous, because no delivery date is given.
options.why: No time period is being asked about here; the fault is that a dissatisfied customer cannot answer at all.

options.text: It is a leading question, because it asks about satisfaction.
options.why: Asking about satisfaction is neutral wording; it is the one-sided list of options that forces a positive answer.

options.text: It creates selection bias, because only customers who ordered can answer.
options.why: Customers who ordered are exactly the group being investigated, so asking them is not a selection fault.

questions.solution_text:
Every option offered is positive, so a customer who was unhappy has nothing to tick.
**Not enough choices.**

questions.question_text: The members of the chess club are surveyed to find out the favourite lunchtime activity of students at the school. Which statement best explains why the sample is unrepresentative?

options.text: Chess club members are far more likely to choose chess than students in general.
The chess club has fewer members than the school has students.
options.why: Every sample is smaller than its population, so being smaller is not what makes this one unfair.

options.text: Some chess club members might not answer the survey honestly.
options.why: Dishonest answers are a separate problem; the sample is unfair because of which students were chosen.

options.text: Chess is a quiet game, so it is hard to survey people while they play.
options.why: Describes a difficulty in collecting the data rather than a reason the group misrepresents the school.

questions.solution_text:
The students surveyed all joined a chess club, so chess is over-represented compared with the whole school.
**The sample favours chess and cannot represent all students' favourite activity.**

questions.question_text: A club committee runs an online poll that any member may choose to answer. Which change would best remove the bias?

options.text: Contact members chosen from the full membership list, instead of letting members choose to reply.
Leave the poll open for another two weeks to collect more responses.
options.why: More responses gathered the same way repeat the same volunteer bias instead of removing it.

options.text: Ask each member who replies to answer a few extra questions.
options.why: Collects more detail from the same self-selected members without reaching those who did not reply.

options.text: Post the poll link on the club's social-media page as well.
options.why: Widens where the link appears, but members still choose for themselves whether to reply.

questions.solution_text:
The bias comes from members choosing themselves, so the fix must take that choice away.
**Contact members chosen from the full membership list.**

questions.question_text: A survey asking how often people shop online is carried out by stopping people inside a shopping centre. What is the most likely effect on the result?

options.text: It will under-estimate how often people shop online.
It will over-estimate how often people shop online.
options.why: Reverses the direction: the people surveyed are the ones who chose to shop in person that day.

options.text: It will give an accurate result, because shoppers use both ways of shopping.
options.why: Assumes the two groups balance out, when the sample is drawn only from people shopping in person.

options.text: It will under-estimate how many people own a computer.
options.why: Changes the variable being measured; the survey asks about online shopping, not computer ownership.

questions.solution_text:
The people surveyed all chose to shop in person, and people who shop mainly online are not in the shopping centre to be asked.
**The result will under-estimate how often people shop online.**

questions.question_text: An online poll on a gaming website receives $80\,000$ responses, and $92\%$ say a new console is the best on sale. Which statement best explains why the result may still be biased?

options.text: Every response came from a gaming-website visitor who chose to reply.
A sample of $80\,000$ is too small to represent all console buyers.
options.why: Eighty thousand responses is a large sample; the size is not the defect, the way they were gathered is.

options.text: The poll should have reported a count instead of a percentage.
options.why: How the result is written down does not change who was asked or how they were chosen.

options.text: The poll is biased only if fewer than half of the site's visitors replied.
options.why: Invents a response-rate threshold; the sample is unrepresentative however many visitors reply.

questions.solution_text:
The respondents are all gaming-website visitors who chose to click the poll, so the same self-selected group is repeated $80\,000$ times.
**A large number of responses does not remove volunteer bias.**
